Namespace mata¶

namespace mata

Main namespace including structs and algorithms for all automata.

In particular, this includes:

  1. Alphabets,

  2. Formula graphs and nodes,

  3. Mintermization,

  4. Closed sets.

Returns name written as a single token of the .mata format.

Quotes the name when it is empty, contains white space, a quote, or a character the reader treats specially ("#@%()!&|\\"), writing an inner @c " as ", the only escape the reader knows. A name ending in \ cannot be quoted this way, because the reader reads the closing " as an escaped quote; such a name never reads back to the same symbol.

class IntAlphabet : public Alphabet
#include <alphabet.hh>

Direct alphabet (also identity alphabet or integer alphabet) using integers as symbols.

This alphabet presumes that all integers are valid symbols. Therefore, calling member functions get_complement() and get_alphabet_symbols() makes no sense in this context and the methods will throw exceptions warning about the inappropriate use of IntAlphabet. If one needs these functions, they should use OnTheFlyAlphabet instead of IntAlphabet.

class EnumAlphabet : public Alphabet
#include <alphabet.hh>

Enumerated alphabet using a set of integers as symbols maintaining a set of specified symbols.

EnumAlphabet is a version of direct (identity) alphabet (does not give names to symbols, their name is their integer value directly). However, unlike IntAlphabet, EnumAlphabet maintains an ordered set of symbols in the alphabet.

Therefore, calling member functions get_complement() and get_alphabet_symbols() makes sense in the context of EnumAlphabet and the functions give the expected results.

Example: 

Alphabet alphabet{ EnumAlphabet{ 0, 4, 6, 8, 9 } };
CHECK(alphabet.translate_symb("6") == 6);
CHECK_THROWS(alphabet.translate_symb("5")); // Throws an exception about an unknown symbol.
CHECK(alphabet.get_complement({ utils::OrdVector<Symbol>{ 0, 6, 9 } }) == utils::OrdVector<Symbol>{ 4, 8 });

class AlphabetLevels
#include <alphabet.hh>

Per-level alphabets for transducer-like automata.

Standalone (does NOT inherit from Alphabet) wrapper holding a vector of std::shared_ptr<Alphabet>, one per level. Operates in one of two modes (see Mode):

  • Global — a single shared alphabet (typically stored in alphabets[0]) applies to every level. The level argument is ignored.

  • MultiLevel — distinct per-level alphabets. The level argument is required and indexes alphabets.

The underlying Alphabet objects are held via std::shared_ptr and can be shared between multiple AlphabetLevels instances (and other automata).

Raw slot access (mode-agnostic).

Bounds-checked access to a raw slot by its index in the underlying vector, ignoring mode.

Unlike for_level, a null entry is returned as-is instead of throwing; only an out-of-range index throws.

See also

std::vector::at.

Public Types

enum class Mode : std::uint8_t

Operating mode of the AlphabetLevels instance.

Values:

enumerator Global

alphabets[0] is used for every level; level argument is ignored.

enumerator MultiLevel

Each level uses its own alphabet from alphabets[level]; level argument is required.

Public Functions

inline explicit AlphabetLevels(std::shared_ptr<Alphabet> alphabet)

Use the same alphabet for every level (Global mode).

Stores a single-element vector and sets mode to Global.

bool operator==(const AlphabetLevels &other) const = default

Equality of two AlphabetLevels instances.

Memberwise comparison of mode and the stored alphabet slots. Slots are std::shared_ptr<Alphabet> and are compared by the pointee’s identity (i.e., whether both slots point to the same underlying Alphabet object), not by the alphabets’ contents, since Alphabet does not support value equality.

inline Mode mode() const noexcept

Current operating mode.

inline void set_global_mode(Level level_for_kept_alphabet = 0)

Switch to Global mode, keeping only the alphabet at level_for_kept_alphabet as the single shared alphabet.

Any other stored alphabets are dropped from AlphabetLevels (the Alphabet objects themselves survive if still referenced elsewhere, since they are held via shared_ptr). Unlike for_level, this never throws due to a missing alphabet: switching an empty instance to Global just leaves it empty.

Parameters:

level_for_kept_alphabet – [in] Level whose alphabet to keep. Ignored when no alphabet is currently stored.

Throws:

std::out_of_range – If level_for_kept_alphabet is out of range and at least one alphabet is stored.

inline void set_global_mode(std::shared_ptr<Alphabet> alphabet)

Switch to Global mode, using alphabet as the new single shared alphabet.

Replaces any previously stored alphabets regardless of how many there were. AlphabetLevels takes shared ownership of alphabet (via std::shared_ptr); it may still be shared with other owners.

Parameters:

alphabet – [in] The alphabet to use for every level.

inline void set_multi_level_mode() noexcept

Switch to MultiLevel mode.

Always safe: MultiLevel places no constraint on the number of stored alphabets. Existing alphabets are kept as-is, now indexed by level (e.g., a single alphabet from Global mode becomes level 0’s alphabet).

inline void set_multi_level_mode(std::vector<std::shared_ptr<Alphabet>> alphabets) noexcept

Switch to MultiLevel mode, using alphabets as the new per-level alphabets.

Replaces any previously stored alphabets regardless of how many there were.

Parameters:

alphabets – [in] The alphabets to use, indexed by level.

Get the complement of symbols with respect to the alphabet for the given level.

bool empty(std::optional<Level> level = std::nullopt) const

Check whether the alphabet for the given level is empty.

In Global mode, always checks alphabets[0] (level argument is ignored). In MultiLevel mode, checks alphabets[level] when level has a value, or returns true iff every underlying alphabet is empty when level is std::nullopt.

void clear(std::optional<Level> level = std::nullopt)

Clear the alphabet for the given level.

In Global mode, always clears alphabets[0] (level argument is ignored, calling clear repeatedly is idempotent on the same alphabet). In MultiLevel mode, clears alphabets[level] when level has a value, or clears every underlying alphabet when level is std::nullopt.

const std::shared_ptr<Alphabet> &for_level(std::optional<Level> level = std::nullopt) const

Get the alphabet assigned to a specific level.

Validated accessor for the internal vector of std::shared_ptr<Alphabet>.

  • In Global mode, alphabets[0] is returned regardless of level.

  • In MultiLevel mode, level must have a value and be a valid index; the corresponding entry must be non-null.

The stored shared ownership token is handed out (never null on return; missing alphabets throw instead), so that callers which need to keep the alphabet alive beyond the lifetime of this AlphabetLevels (or beyond the next mutation of its slots) can simply copy the returned std::shared_ptr. Callers which only read the alphabet should dereference the returned reference directly (*levels.for_level(level)), which costs no reference-count update. The non-const overload additionally allows replacing the alphabet stored for level.

Parameters:

level – [in] Level whose alphabet should be returned (required in MultiLevel mode).

Throws:

std::runtime_error – If level is missing in MultiLevel mode, out of range, or the entry is null.

Returns:

Non-null std::shared_ptr to the alphabet assigned to level.

Per-level alphabets.

Is no final state reachable from any initial state?

A plain breadth-first search over a visited bit vector that stops at the first final state. This is a pure graph property; whether it coincides with the emptiness of the accepted language (or relation) is a fact about the concrete automaton class, so the leaves expose it under their own names (e.g. mata::nfa::Nfa::is_lang_empty_scc()).

Returns:

true <-> no accepting path exists.

bool is_acyclic() const

Is the automaton graph acyclic?

Returns:

true <-> Automaton graph is acyclic.

template<typename Self> bool is_identical (this const Self &self, const Self &other)

Check if this is structuralry identical to other.

Compares only delta, initial and final. This is exact structural equality, including state numbering (so even stronger than isomorphism), essentially only useful for testing purposes.

Note

Templated on Self (deducing this) so that only same-type comparisons compile.

Parameters:

other – [in] The other automaton to compare with.

Returns:

true iff the structural parts of this and other are identical.

template<typename Self> Self & trim (this Self &self, nfa::StateRenaming *state_renaming=nullptr)

Remove unreachable and non-terminating states in-place.

Remaining states are renumbered densely in ascending order.

Note

A state is reachable when the state is the endpoint of a path starting from an initial state. A state is terminating when the state is the starting point of a path ending in a final state.

Note

Every remaining state therefore lies on an accepting path: after trimming, the language is empty iff initial is empty, which is cheaper to test than is_lang_empty().

Note

Reached only through a leaf’s own one-line trim(), on *this, so an lvalue Self suffices here.

Parameters:

state_renaming – [out] Mapping of trimmed states to new states.

Returns:

this after trimming.

template<typename Self> bool is_lang_empty (this const Self &self, nfa::Run *cex=nullptr)

Check whether no accepting path exists, recording a witness in cex when one does.

Parameters:

cex – [out] Counter-example path (and, via the leaf’s get_word_for_path(), word) for a case an accepting path exists.

Returns:

true if no accepting path exists, false otherwise.

class FormulaGraph

A transition formula as a tree whose nodes are the operators and operands of the formula.

class IntermediateAut
#include <inter-aut.hh>

Structure for a general intermediate representation of parsed automaton.

It contains information about type of automata, type of naming of nodes, symbols and states and type of alphabet. It contains also the transitions formula and formula for initial and final states. The formulas are represented as tree where nodes are either operands or operators.

Public Types

So far we support nondeterministic finite automata (NFA) and nondeterministic finite transducers (NFT).

enumerator Nft
enum class Naming : std::uint8_t

The possible kinds of naming of items in sets of states, nodes, or symbols.

It implies how the given set is defined. Naming could be automatic (all things in formula not belonging to other sets will be assigned to a set with automatic naming), marker based (everything beginning with q is a state, with s is a symbol, with n is a node), or enumerated (the given set is defined by enumeration). There are two special cases used for alphabet - symbols could be any character (CHARS) or anything from utf (UTF).

Operations on NFAs/NFTs used for string constraint solving.

Functions

std::set<Word> get_shortest_words(const Nfa &nfa)

Get shortest words (regarding their length) of the automaton using BFS.

Returns:

Set of shortest words.

std::optional<std::set<Word>> get_longest_words(const Nfa &nfa)

Get the longest words (regarding their length) of the automaton.

The language has longest words iff it is finite, i.e., iff no cycle passes through a useful state (a state reachable from an initial state that reaches a final state). Cycles through useless states are allowed. Every symbol, epsilon included, counts as one letter, as in get_shortest_words().

Costs O(|Q| + |delta|) to compute the length of the longest words from every state, and then a depth-first search over macrostates that follows only the transitions on some longest accepting path, so every branch of the search ends in a word to report and every word is reported once, however many accepting paths spell it.

Returns:

Set of the longest words (empty if the language is empty), or std::nullopt if the language is infinite.

std::optional<std::vector<Word>> get_words_of_lengths(const Nft &nft, const std::vector<unsigned> &lengths)

Get the accepting words for each tape of nft with specific lengths.

This function finds such an accepting word of nft that for each tape i, the word on this tape (on the ith index of resulting vector) has the length lengths[i].

The search runs over configurations (state, number of symbols written on each tape), so it terminates on epsilon cycles and costs O(|delta| * prod(lengths[i] + 1)) instead of being exponential in the lengths.

Parameters:

  • nft – Transducer whose accepting words we are looking for

  • lengths – The lengths of the words of each tape (size of lengths == the levels of nft)

Throws:

std::invalid_argument – When lengths does not have one entry per level of nft, when nft has jump transitions, or when lengths spans more configurations than can be indexed.

Returns:

std::optional<std::vector<Word>> Either the resulting words of tapes, or std::nullopt if such words of specific lengths do not exist

The function returns a set of pairs <u,v> where for each such a pair there is a word with length u+k*v for all ks. The disjunction of such formulae of all pairs hence precisely describe lengths of all words in the automaton.

namespace seg_nfa

Segment Automata including structs and algorithms.

These are automata whose state space can be split into several segments connected by ε-transitions in a chain. No other ε-transitions are allowed. As a consequence, no ε-transitions can appear in a cycle. Segment automaton can have initial states only in the first segment and final states only in the last segment.

Typedefs

Number of visited epsilons.

Projection of VisitedEpsilonsNumberMap to sorted keys (in descending order).

using Noodle = std::vector<NoodleSegment>

A noodle is represented as a sequence of segments created as if there was exactly one ε-transition between each two consecutive segments.

using SegmentWithEpsilonsCounter = std::pair<NoodleSegment, VisitedEpsilonsCounterVector>

Segment with a counter of visited epsilons.

using NoodleWithEpsilonsCounter = std::vector<SegmentWithEpsilonsCounter>

Noodles as segments enriched with EpsCntMap.

using TransducerNoodle = std::vector<TransducerNoodleElement>

Functions

void segs_one_initial_final(const std::vector<Nfa> &segments, bool include_empty, const State &unused_state, std::map<std::pair<State, State>, NoodleSegment> &out)

segs_one_initial_final

segments_one_initial_final[init, final] is the segment of one of the segments such that init and final are one of the initial and final states of the segment, i.e. the language from init to final in the segment; also segments_one_initial_final[unused_state, final] is used for the first segment (where we always want all initial states, only final state changes) and segments_one_initial_final[init, unused_state] is similarly for the last segment. All pairs of one final state share one automaton (see NoodleSegment); the first segment, whose pairs differ in the final state only, gets a single initial state by unifying its initial states. The map is ordered so that all pairs of one initial state are contiguous: noodlify_mult_eps() visits them with one range scan instead of probing every final state.

std::vector<Noodle> noodlify_for_equation(const std::vector<std::reference_wrapper<Nfa>> &lhs_automata, const Nfa &rhs_automaton, bool include_empty = false, const ParameterMap &params = {{"reduce", "false"}})

Create noodles for left and right side of equation.

Segment automaton is a chain of finite automata (segments) connected via ε-transitions. A noodle is a copy of the segment automaton with exactly one ε-transition between each two consecutive segments.

Mata cannot work with equations, queries etc. Hence, we compute the noodles for the equation, but represent the equation in a way that libMata understands. The left side automata represent the left side of the equation and the right automaton represents the right side of the equation. To create noodles, we need a segment automaton representing the intersection. That can be achieved by computing a product of both sides. First, the left side has to be concatenated over an epsilon transitions into a single automaton to compute the intersection on, though.

Parameters:

  • lhs_automata – [in] Sequence of segment automata for left side of an equation to noodlify.

  • rhs_automaton – [in] Segment automaton for right side of an equation to noodlify.

  • include_empty – [in] Whether to also include empty noodles.

  • params – [in] Additional parameters for the noodlification:

    • ”reduce”: “false”, “forward”, “backward”, “bidirectional”; Execute forward, backward or bidirectional simulation minimization before noodlification.

Returns:

A list of all (non-empty) noodles.

struct NoodleSegment
#include <strings.hh>

A segment of a noodle: the part of a segment automaton between one of its initial states and one of its final states.

automaton is the reduced part of the segment automaton that reaches the final state, shared by all segments that end in that final state; the segment is the language of initial in it. The initial states of automaton itself are hence not those of the segment. The parts of one final state overlap almost completely, so sharing them keeps one automaton per final state instead of one per pair of an initial and a final state.

struct TransducerNoodleElement
#include <strings.hh>
struct NoodleOrder
#include <strings.hh>

The order in which the noodlify_*_lazy() functions emit the noodles.

The search is depth-first over the segments; at every node it orders the candidates for the next segment (the pairs of an initial and a final state of it). The order is greedy: a candidate ranked first leads to the next noodle, not necessarily to the best noodle overall.

bool is_intersection_empty(const Nfa &lhs, const Nfa &rhs, Run *witness = nullptr, Symbol first_epsilon = EPSILON)

Check whether the language intersection of two NFAs is empty, without materializing the product.

Explores reachable pairs (state_of_lhs, state_of_rhs) directly and stops at the first pair that is final in both automata. The traversal moves on shared symbols in both automata at once and lets a symbol at or above first_epsilon move one side only – the same semantics that intersection(lhs, rhs, first_epsilon) materializes, but only up to the first witness.

Parameters:

  • lhs – [in] First NFA.

  • rhs – [in] Second NFA.

  • witness – [out] When not null and the intersection is nonempty, receives a word accepted by both automata (some valid word, not necessarily the shortest). One-sided epsilon moves (symbols at or above first_epsilon) are stripped. With the default first_epsilon, the word replays in both automata with Nfa::is_in_lang(witness, use_epsilon = true); that replay follows only EPSILON transitions, so with a custom first_epsilon, relabel the symbols at or above it to EPSILON before replaying.

  • first_epsilon – [in] Smallest symbol treated as a one-sided (epsilon) move.

Returns:

True iff there is no word accepted by both lhs and rhs.

Nfa left_quotient(const Nfa &nfa, const Nfa &prefixes, Symbol first_epsilon = EPSILON)

Compute the left quotient of the language of nfa by the language of prefixes.

The left quotient (derivative by a language) is { w | there is u in L(prefixes) with u.w in L(nfa) }: the words of nfa with a prefix from prefixes removed. With prefixes accepting a single word u, this is the Brzozowski derivative of nfa by u.

The result is nfa with its initial states replaced by the states of nfa reachable by reading a word of prefixes. These are found by exploring the reachable pairs (state_of_prefixes, state_of_nfa) directly, without materializing the product, and pairs with a useless state of prefixes are never explored. The result is not trimmed: call Nfa::trim() to remove the states no longer reachable.

Symbols at or above first_epsilon move one side only, as in intersection(lhs, rhs, first_epsilon), so epsilon transitions of both automata are supported. The epsilon transitions of nfa are kept in the result.

Parameters:

  • nfa – [in] NFA whose language is quotiented.

  • prefixes – [in] NFA accepting the prefixes to remove.

  • first_epsilon – [in] Smallest symbol treated as a one-sided (epsilon) move.

Returns:

NFA for the left quotient of nfa by prefixes.

Nfa left_quotient(Nfa &&nfa, const Nfa &prefixes, Symbol first_epsilon = EPSILON)

Compute the left quotient of the language of nfa by the language of prefixes, consuming nfa.

The transitions of nfa are moved into the result instead of copied. nfa and prefixes may be the same automaton. nfa is moved from.

See also

left_quotient(const Nfa&, const Nfa&, Symbol)

Nfa right_quotient(const Nfa &nfa, const Nfa &suffixes, Symbol first_epsilon = EPSILON)

Compute the right quotient of the language of nfa by the language of suffixes.

The right quotient is { u | there is w in L(suffixes) with u.w in L(nfa) }: the words of nfa with a suffix from suffixes removed.

The result is nfa with its final states replaced by the states of nfa from which nfa accepts a word of suffixes. These are found as in left_quotient(), but backward: pairs of a state of the reverted suffixes and a state of nfa are explored from the final states of both, moving nfa against its transitions over an index of predecessors, without reverting nfa or materializing the product. The result is not trimmed: call Nfa::trim() to remove the states that no longer reach a final state.

Symbols at or above first_epsilon move one side only, as in intersection(lhs, rhs, first_epsilon), so epsilon transitions of both automata are supported. The epsilon transitions of nfa are kept in the result.

Parameters:

  • nfa – [in] NFA whose language is quotiented.

  • suffixes – [in] NFA accepting the suffixes to remove.

  • first_epsilon – [in] Smallest symbol treated as a one-sided (epsilon) move.

Returns:

NFA for the right quotient of nfa by suffixes.

Nfa right_quotient(Nfa &&nfa, const Nfa &suffixes, Symbol first_epsilon = EPSILON)

Compute the right quotient of the language of nfa by the language of suffixes, consuming nfa.

The transitions of nfa are moved into the result instead of copied. nfa and suffixes may be the same automaton. nfa is moved from.

Nfa complement(const Nfa &aut, const Alphabet &alphabet, const ParameterMap &params = {{"algorithm", "classical"}})

Compute automaton accepting complement of aut.

The complement is a language over alphabet only: transitions over symbols outside of alphabet are dropped and the words of the result therefore never contain any other symbol.

Parameters:

  • aut – [in] Automaton whose complement to compute.

  • alphabet – [in] Alphabet used for complementation.

  • params – [in] Optional parameters to control the complementation algorithm:

    • ”algorithm”:

      • ”classical”: The classical algorithm determinizes the automaton, makes it complete, and swaps final and non-final states. An already deterministic automaton is complemented directly, without determinizing it first.

      • ”brzozowski”: The Brzozowski algorithm determinizes the automaton using Brzozowski minimization, makes it complete, and swaps final and non-final states.

Returns:

Complemented automaton.

Nfa complement(const Nfa &aut, const utils::OrdVector<Symbol> &symbols, const ParameterMap &params = {{"algorithm", "classical"}})

Compute automaton accepting complement of aut.

This overloaded version complements over an already created ordered set of symbols instead of an alphabet. This is a more efficient solution in case you already have symbols precomputed or want to complement multiple automata over the same set of symbols: the function does not need to compute the ordered set of symbols from the alphabet again (and for each automaton).

Parameters:

  • aut – [in] Automaton whose complement to compute.

  • symbols – [in] Symbols to complement over. Transitions over any other symbol are dropped, the complement is a language over symbols only.

  • params – [in] Optional parameters to control the complementation algorithm:

    • ”algorithm”:

      • ”classical”: The classical algorithm determinizes the automaton, makes it complete, and swaps final and non-final states. An already deterministic automaton is complemented directly, without determinizing it first.

      • ”brzozowski”: The Brzozowski algorithm determinizes the automaton using Brzozowski minimization, makes it complete, and swaps final and non-final states.

Returns:

Complemented automaton.

Nfa complement(Nfa &&aut, const utils::OrdVector<Symbol> &symbols, const ParameterMap &params = {{"algorithm", "classical"}})

This overloaded version accepts an rvalue reference and complements in place when the input is deterministic and the “classical” algorithm is requested, avoiding an unnecessary copy of a temporary automaton.

  • params – [in] Optional parameters to control the minimization algorithm:

    • ”algorithm”:

      • ”auto” (default): determinize the automaton if it is not deterministic, trim it, and run Hopcroft minimization. An automaton with an empty language is returned as a single non-final initial state.

      • ”hopcroft”: Hopcroft minimization; the input must be a trimmed deterministic automaton.

      • ”brzozowski”: revert, determinize, revert, determinize. Accepts any automaton, but determinizes twice and can therefore blow up exponentially, even on an input that already is a trimmed deterministic automaton.

Returns:

Minimal deterministic automaton.

Nfa determinize(const Nfa &aut, std::unordered_map<StateSet, State> *subset_map = nullptr, std::optional<std::function<bool(const Nfa&, State, const StateSet&)>> macrostate_discover = std::nullopt, const utils::OrdVector<Symbol> *restrict_to_symbols = nullptr, const ParameterMap &params = {{"algorithm", "four_russians"}})

Determinize automaton.

Todo:

: TODO: Add support for specifying first epsilon symbol and compute epsilon closure during determinization.

Note

With the same reduction, both give the same DFA, but they may number its states differently.

Parameters:

  • aut – [in] Automaton to determinize.

  • subset_map – [out] Map that maps sets of states of input automaton to states of determinized automaton.

  • macrostate_discover – [in] Callback event handler for discovering a new macrostate for the first time. The parameters are the determinized NFA constructed so far, the current macrostate, and the set of the original states corresponding to the macrostate. Return true if the determinization should continue, and false if the determinization should stop and return only the determinized NFA constructed so far.

  • restrict_to_symbols – [in] When not nullptr, determinize over these symbols only. Transitions over any other symbol are ignored, so the macrostates reachable only over such a transition are never constructed. The caller gets the determinization of aut with its transitions restricted to restrict_to_symbols.

  • params – [in] Optional parameters to control the determinization algorithm:

    • ”algorithm” (required in params, which is {“algorithm”: “four_russians”} by default):

      • ”four_russians”: The “Four Russians” subset construction, see algorithms::determinize_four_russians().

      • ”classical”: The classical subset construction, see algorithms::determinize_classical().

    • ”reduction”:

      • ”none” (default): No reduction.

      • ”bisimulation”, “simulation”, “adaptive”: A smaller DFA for the same language, not always minimal, see algorithms::DeterminizationReduction. It is no longer the subset construction, so in subset_map, merged states appear as one of them, and macrostate_discover is not allowed.

Returns:

Determinized automaton.

bool are_equivalent(const Nfa &lhs, const Nfa &rhs, const ParameterMap &params = {{"algorithm", "antichains"}}, Run *cex = nullptr)

Perform equivalence check of two NFAs: lhs and rhs.

The current implementation of Nfa does not accept input alphabet. For this reason, an alphabet has to be created from all transitions each time an operation on alphabet is called. When calling this function, the alphabet has to be computed first.

Hence, this function is less efficient than its alternative taking already defined alphabet as its parameter. That way, alphabet has to be computed only once, as opposed to the current ad-hoc construction of the alphabet. The use of the alternative with defined alphabet should be preferred.

Epsilon transitions are removed from copies of the operands that have them.

Parameters:

  • lhs – [in] First automaton to concatenate.

  • rhs – [in] Second automaton to concatenate.

  • params – [in] Optional parameters to control the equivalence check algorithm:

    • ”algorithm”: “naive”, “antichains” (Default: “antichains”)

  • cex – [out] If not null and lhs and rhs are not equivalent, filled with a witness word: a word in the language of one of lhs/rhs but not the other. Cleared (empty word and path) if lhs and rhs are equivalent.

Returns:

True if lhs and rhs are equivalent, false otherwise.

Nfa revert(const Nfa &aut)

Reverting the automaton by a counting sort (see Delta::reverted()): much faster than the three insertion-based variants below, which are kept for benchmarking.

Nfa fragile_revert(const Nfa &aut)

This revert algorithm is fragile, uses low level accesses to Nfa and static data structures, and is potentially dangerous when there are used symbols with large numbers (allocates an array indexed by symbols). It is asymptotically faster, however. For somewhat dense automata, the performance is the same or a little bit slower than simple_revert otherwise. Not affected by pre-reserving vectors.

Nfa simple_revert(const Nfa &aut)

Reverting the automaton by a simple algorithm, which does a lot of random access addition to Post and Move. Much affected by pre-reserving vectors.

Nfa somewhat_simple_revert(const Nfa &aut)

Reverting the automaton by a modification of the simple algorithm. It replaces random access addition to SymbolPost by push_back and sorting later, so far seems the slowest of all, except on dense automata, where it is almost as slow as simple_revert. Candidate for removal.

Get any arbitrary accepted word in the language difference of nfa_included without nfa_excluded.

The language difference automaton is lazily constructed without computing the whole determinized automata and the complememt of nfa_excluded. The algorithm returns an arbitrary word from the language difference constructed until the first macrostate with a final state in the original states in nfa_included and without any corresponding final states in nfa_excluded is encountered.

Nfa trim(const Nfa &nfa, StateRenaming *state_renaming = nullptr, std::optional<std::reference_wrapper<const utils::SparseSet<State>>> initial_states = std::nullopt, std::optional<std::reference_wrapper<const utils::SparseSet<State>>> final_states = std::nullopt)

Creates a new NFA with inaccessible (unreachable) and not co-accessible (non-terminating) states removed from the input NFA nfa.

Remove states which are not accessible (unreachable; state is accessible when the state is the endpoint of a path starting from an initial state) or not co-accessible (non-terminating; state is co-accessible when the state is the starting point of a path ending in a final state).

The out-of-place trimming constructs the trimmed NFA directly from the useful states, so it does not copy the transitions of the useless states only to discard them. When many states are useless, this is faster than copying the NFA and trimming the copy in place. The alphabet and the attributes of nfa are carried over to the result.

Note

The states in the returned NFA are renumbered.

Parameters:

  • nfa – NFA to trim.

  • state_renaming – [out] Mapping of trimmed states to new states.

  • initial_states – Optional set of initial states to consider instead of nfa.initial_states. If std::nullopt, uses initial states of nfa.

  • final_states – Optional set of final states to consider instead of nfa.final_states. If std::nullopt, uses final states of nfa.

Returns:

A new NFA from nfa after trimming.

Structure represents a post of a single symbol: a set of target states in transitions.

struct PostWorkspace¶
#include <delta.hh>

Reusable scratch buffers of the successor and epsilon-closure computations.

The buffers only ever hold states the call reaches, so a call costs time proportional to what it visits, never to the number of states of the automaton. A fresh workspace per call is therefore cheap; reusing one across calls also saves the buffer allocations.

A workspace belongs to one call or to one explicit caller context. It must never be shared between threads, and in particular it must never be a function-local static: that is the data race of #731.

class Delta
#include <delta.hh>

Delta is a data structure for representing transition relation.

Transition is represented as a triple Transition(source state, symbol, target state). Move is the part (symbol, target state), specified for a single source state. Its underlying data structure is vector of StatePost classes. Each index to the vector corresponds to one source state, that is, a number for a certain state is an index to the vector of state posts. Transition relation (delta) in Mata stores a set of transitions in a four-level hierarchical structure: Delta, StatePost, SymbolPost, and a set of target states. A vector of ‘StatePost’s indexed by a source states on top, where the StatePost for a state ‘q’ (whose number is ‘q’ and it is the index to the vector of ‘StatePost’s) stores a set of ‘Move’s from the source state ‘q’. Namely, ‘StatePost’ has a vector of ‘SymbolPost’s, where each ‘SymbolPost’ stores a symbol ‘a’ and a vector of target states of ‘a’-moves from state ‘q’. ‘SymbolPost’s are ordered by the symbol, target states are ordered by the state number.

Parameters:

Returns:

State post of source.

StatePost &mutable_state_post(State source)

Get mutable (non-constant) reference to the state post of source.

The function allows modifying the state post.

BEWARE, IT HAS A SIDE EFFECT.

If we try to access a state post of a source which is present in the automaton as an initial/final state, yet does not have allocated space in Delta, a new state post for source will be allocated along with all state posts for all previous states. This in turn may cause that the entire post data structure is re-allocated. Iterators to Delta will get invalidated. Use the constant ‘state_post()’ is possible. Or, to prevent the side effect from causing issues, one might want to make sure that posts of all states in the automaton are allocated, e.g., write an NFA method that allocate Delta for all states of the NFA. The reference may be used for edits only until the next query of the transition count of this delta: num_of_transitions(), empty(), or any operation on the owning automaton, which may call them. The query takes the edits made so far into account; edits made through the reference after it are not seen by the cached count. Obtain the reference again after such a query.

Parameters:

source[in] – Source state of a state post to access.

Returns:

State post of source.

void add(State source, SymbolPost &&symbol_post)

Add a whole, already sorted symbol post to source.

The targets of symbol_post are merged into the post of source in one linear pass, instead of one binary search and one vector shift per target as repeated add() would do.

void add(std::vector<Transition> &&transitions)

Add transitions given in an arbitrary order.

Sorts transitions by (source, symbol, target) and deduplicates them once, then writes whole symbol posts, instead of searching and shifting per transition as repeated add() does. An empty delta gets the transitions bucketed by source in linear time, which leaves only the transitions of each source to sort. Duplicates collapse and states up to the largest mentioned one are allocated, exactly as with repeated add().

Parameters:

transitions – [inout] Transitions to add; consumed.

Delta &append_shifted(const Delta &other, State offset)

Append the state posts of other, shifting every state of other by offset.

The state posts of other become the state posts of offset, offset+1, … of this, and every target of other is increased by offset. The shift is monotone, so the target sets stay sorted and are never re-sorted. State posts up to offset are allocated (as empty posts) first, so the appended posts land exactly at offset.

This is the primitive behind the union and the concatenation of two automata, where the right operand’s states are the left operand’s states shifted by a constant.

Parameters:

  • other – [in] Delta to append; appending a delta to itself takes one controlled snapshot.

  • offset – [in] State offset to shift other by; must be at least num_of_states().

Throws:

std::overflow_error – If offset+other.num_of_states() does not fit into State.

Returns:

this after the append.

Delta &append_shifted(Delta &&other, State offset)

Append the state posts of other, shifting every state of other by offset, consuming other.

Same result as append_shifted(const Delta&, State), but the state posts of other are moved instead of copied, so the append allocates nothing per post. other is left empty.

Parameters:

  • other – [inout] Delta to consume; left empty.

  • offset – [in] State offset to shift other by; must be at least num_of_states().

Throws:

std::overflow_error – If offset+other.num_of_states() does not fit into State.

Returns:

this after the append.

Delta reverted(size_t num_of_states) const

Reverse every transition: the target of each (source, symbol, target) becomes the source and vice versa.

Built by a counting sort: the incoming transitions of every state are counted, prefix-summed into CSR offsets, and (symbol, source) pairs scattered into one slice per target state; sorting each slice by (symbol, source) yields exactly the state post of the reversed state, emitted with exact capacity. There is no per-transition binary search and no symbol-indexed array, so the cost is linear in the number of states and transitions (plus the per-slice sort), regardless of the largest symbol used.

As with building the result by repeated add(target, symbol, source), a target beyond num_of_states extends the result to cover it; states without incoming transitions get an empty post.

Parameters:

num_of_states – [in] Number of posts of the result; the state domain of the automaton being reverted.

Returns:

The reversed delta.

inline uint64_t mutation_epoch() const

Number of mutating calls performed on this delta so far.

Increases by one per mutating public call, including mutable_state_post(), which cannot observe what the caller does with the returned reference; an assignment moves it past the epochs of both operands. Holders of data derived from the delta can cache the epoch together with the value and recompute once the epoch moves. Copy and move construction carry the epoch of their source; a moved-from delta is left empty with a new epoch. The value is only ever compared with another value read from the same delta.

class DeltaBuilder
#include <delta.hh>

Append-only builder of a Delta whose transitions are produced in order.

Delta::add() is the right primitive for one unpredictable edit: it searches for the symbol and for the position of the target and shifts the vectors. An algorithm that already produces its output in order pays those searches for nothing. The builder promises the order instead, so every value is written at the end in constant time, and the finished posts are moved into the delta once.

The caller must keep these invariants; each is checked by MATA_ASSERT in Debug builds and assumed in Release builds:

  • begin_state() is called with strictly increasing source states;

  • begin_symbol() is called with strictly increasing symbols within one source state;

  • push_sorted_target() is called with strictly increasing targets within one symbol;

  • begin_symbol() / begin_state() are closed by finish_symbol() / finish_state() before the next one begins, and a symbol post with no target is not emitted;

  • no reference obtained from the builder survives finish_state().

Duplicate transitions are a precondition violation, not a silently collapsed input: use Delta::add(std::vector<Transition>&&) for data that may be unordered or contain duplicates.

Public Functions

num_of_states_hint – [in] Expected number of states, used to reserve the state posts up front.

bool is_deterministic() const

Test whether an automaton is deterministic.

I.e., whether it has exactly one initial state and every state has at most one outgoing transition over every symbol. Checks the whole automaton, not only the reachable part

bool is_minimal() const

Test whether the automaton is a minimal deterministic automaton of its language.

Minimal in the sense of the result of ‘minimize()’: deterministic, trimmed (every state reachable and co-reachable, so the transition function may be partial and a sink state counts as redundant), and with no two equivalent states. The empty language is minimal only as a single non-final initial state without transitions. Runs in O(a*n*log(n)) by Hopcroft partition refinement.

std::set<Word> get_words(size_t max_length) const

Get the set of all words in the language of the automaton whose length is <= max_length.

If you have an automaton with finite language (can be checked using is_acyclic), you can get all words by calling get_words(aut.num_of_states())

The search goes over words, not over paths: the states reachable by a word are kept together as one macrostate, so the work is bounded by the number of distinct words of length <= max_length that have a run in the automaton, no matter how many accepting paths each of them has.

std::optional<Word> get_word_from_complement(const Alphabet *alphabet = nullptr) const

Get any arbitrary accepted word in the language of the complement of the automaton.

The automaton is lazily determinized and made complete. The algorithm returns an arbitrary word from the complemented NFA constructed until the first macrostate without any final states in the original automaton is encountered.

Transitions over symbols outside of the chosen alphabet are ignored; the automaton is complemented only with respect to the symbols of alphabet and the returned word never contains any other symbol.

Parameters:

alphabet – [in] Alphabet to use for computing the complement. If nullptr, uses this->alphabet when defined, otherwise uses this->delta.get_used_symbols().

Pre:

The automaton does not contain any epsilon transitions. TODO: Support lazy epsilon closure?

Returns:

An arbitrary word from the complemented automaton, or std::nullopt if the automaton is universal on the chosen set of symbols for the complement.

bool make_complete(const Alphabet *alphabet = nullptr, std::optional<State> sink_state = std::nullopt)

Make NFA complete in place.

For each state 0,…,this->num_of_states()-1, add transitions with “missing” symbols from alphabet (symbols that do not occur on transitions from given state) to sink_state. If sink_state does not belong to the NFA, it is added to it, but only in the case that some transition to sink_state was added. In the case that NFA does not contain any states, this function does nothing.

Parameters:

  • alphabet – [in] Alphabet to use for computing “missing” symbols. If nullptr, use this->alphabet when defined, otherwise use this->delta.get_used_symbols().

  • sink_state – [in] The state into which new transitions are added. If std::nullopt, add a new sink state.

Returns:

true if a new transition was added to the NFA.

bool make_complete(const utils::OrdVector<Symbol> &symbols, std::optional<State> sink_state = std::nullopt)

Make NFA complete in place.

For each state 0,…,this->num_of_states()-1, add transitions with “missing” symbols from alphabet (symbols that do not occur on transitions from given state) to sink_state. If sink_state does not belong to the NFA, it is added to it, but only in the case that some transition to sink_state was added. In the case that NFA does not contain any states, this function does nothing.

This overloaded version is a more efficient version which does not need to compute the set of symbols to complete to from the alphabet. Prefer this version when you already have the set of symbols precomputed or plan to complete multiple automata over the same set of symbols.

Parameters:

  • symbols – [in] Symbols to compute “missing” symbols from.

  • sink_state – [in] The state into which new transitions are added. If std::nullopt, add a new sink state.

Returns:

true if a new transition was added to the NFA.

bool has_no_accepting_path() const

Is no final state reachable from any initial state?

A plain breadth-first search over a visited bit vector that stops at the first final state. This is a pure graph property; whether it coincides with the emptiness of the accepted language (or relation) is a fact about the concrete automaton class, so the leaves expose it under their own names (e.g. mata::nfa::Nfa::is_lang_empty_scc()).

Returns:

true <-> no accepting path exists.

template<typename Self> bool is_identical (this const Self &self, const Self &other)

Check if this is structuralry identical to other.

Compares only delta, initial and final. This is exact structural equality, including state numbering (so even stronger than isomorphism), essentially only useful for testing purposes.

Note

Templated on Self (deducing this) so that only same-type comparisons compile.

Parameters:

other – [in] The other automaton to compare with.

Returns:

true iff the structural parts of this and other are identical.

template<typename Self> Self & trim (this Self &self, nfa::StateRenaming *state_renaming=nullptr)

Remove unreachable and non-terminating states in-place.

Remaining states are renumbered densely in ascending order.

Note

A state is reachable when the state is the endpoint of a path starting from an initial state. A state is terminating when the state is the starting point of a path ending in a final state.

Note

Every remaining state therefore lies on an accepting path: after trimming, the language is empty iff initial is empty, which is cheaper to test than is_lang_empty().

Note

Reached only through a leaf’s own one-line trim(), on *this, so an lvalue Self suffices here.

Parameters:

state_renaming – [out] Mapping of trimmed states to new states.

Returns:

this after trimming.

template<typename Self> bool is_lang_empty (this const Self &self, nfa::Run *cex=nullptr)

Check whether no accepting path exists, recording a witness in cex when one does.

true if no accepting path exists, false otherwise.

namespace algorithms¶

Concrete NFA implementations of algorithms, such as complement, inclusion, or universality checking.

Enums

enum class DeterminizationReduction : std::uint8_t¶

Reduction of the DFA of determinize_four_russians() and determinize_classical() to a smaller DFA for the same language, not always minimal. There is no real winner, but based on benchmarks, Adaptive is the best choice for general use.

Values:

enumerator None¶

No reduction.

enumerator Bisimulation¶

Merge bisimilar states. Fast.

enumerator Simulation¶

Also use the simulation. Smaller DFAs, but memory quadratic in the number of states.

enumerator Adaptive¶

Start with Bisimulation, and switch to Simulation if the DFA turns out large.

Functions

Nfa determinize_four_russians(const Nfa &aut, const FourRussiansOptions &options = {}, std::unordered_map<StateSet, State> *subset_map = nullptr, std::optional<std::function<bool(const Nfa&, State, const StateSet&)>> macrostate_discover = std::nullopt, const utils::OrdVector<Symbol> *restrict_to_symbols = nullptr)¶

Determinize automaton by the “Four Russians” subset construction.

This is the “Four Russians” technique of Arlazarov, Dinic, Kronrod and Faradzev (1970), applied lazily.

Gives the DFA of determinize_classical() up to the numbering of the states, usually much faster on large automata. The default algorithm of determinize(). The NFA states are cut into blocks, and the post of each combination of states of a block is computed once, when it first occurs, and kept in a table. The post of a macrostate is then a union over its blocks instead of its states.

With a reduction, it gives a smaller DFA for the same language, not always minimal. A reduction usually lowers the memory usage. Its effect on the time varies: inputs whose DFA shrinks a lot are much faster, others may be slower.

const Nfa dfa = algorithms::determinize_four_russians(aut);
const Nfa smaller = algorithms::determinize_four_russians(aut, {.reduction = DeterminizationReduction::Adaptive});
Parameters:

  • aut – [in] Automaton to determinize.

  • options – [in] Block size and reduction.

  • subset_map – [out] Map that maps sets of states of input automaton to states of determinized automaton (with a reduction, merged states appear as one of them).

  • macrostate_discover – [in] Callback event handler for discovering a new macrostate for the first time, as in determinize(). Not allowed with a reduction.

  • restrict_to_symbols – [in] When not nullptr, determinize over these symbols only, as in determinize().

Throws:

std::invalid_argument – for an invalid block size, or for a reduction with macrostate_discover.

Returns:

Determinized automaton.

Nfa determinize_classical(const Nfa &aut, std::unordered_map<StateSet, State> *subset_map = nullptr, std::optional<std::function<bool(const Nfa&, State, const StateSet&)>> macrostate_discover = std::nullopt, const utils::OrdVector<Symbol> *restrict_to_symbols = nullptr, DeterminizationReduction reduction = DeterminizationReduction::None)¶

Returns:

Minimized automaton.

Nfa minimize_hopcroft(const Nfa &dfa_trimmed)¶

Hopcroft minimization of automata.

Based on the algorithm from the paper: “Efficient Minimization of DFAs With Partial Transition Functions” by Antti Valmari and Petri Lehtinen. The algorithm works in O(a*n*log(n)) time and O(m+n+a) space, where: n is the number of states, a is the size of the alphabet, and m is the number of transitions. [https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1016/j.ipl.2011.12.004]

Parameters:

dfa_trimmed – [in] Deterministic automaton without useless states. Perform trimming before calling this function.

Returns:

Minimized deterministic automaton.

Nfa minimize_auto(const Nfa &aut)¶

Minimization that picks the algorithm from the shape of the input.

Determinizes aut when it is not deterministic already, trims it, and runs Hopcroft minimization on the result. Brzozowski minimization is never picked: it determinizes twice, so it can blow up exponentially even on an input that is already a trimmed DFA, where Hopcroft is O(a*n*log(n)). An automaton with an empty language is returned as a single non-final initial state with no transitions.

Parameters:

aut – [in] Automaton to be minimized.

Returns:

Minimal deterministic automaton.

std::vector<State> identical_successor_classes(const Automaton &aut, size_t num_of_states, std::span<const Level> levels = {})¶

Classes of states that have the same finality, the same level, and, over every symbol, successors in the same classes.

Starts from the identity and merges states with identical successors, then states whose successors became identical by the merge, until nothing merges. Every merge joins classes with the same successors, so the partition stays a bisimulation and the quotient keeps the forward simulation of every state. It is far cheaper than the simulation itself: the first pass hashes each state post once, and after it only the classes of the predecessors of the states of an absorbed class are hashed again. The classes are numbered in the order of their smallest states.

Parameters:

  • aut – [in] Automaton whose states to classify.

  • num_of_states – [in] Number of states of aut.

  • levels – [in] Level of each state of a transducer. States past its end, and all states of an NFA, for which it is empty, are on level 0.

Returns:

The class of each state; the number of classes is one past the largest class.

inline uint64_t macrostate_signature(const StateSet &macrostate)¶

Signature of a macrostate: the OR of 1 << (q % 64) over its states q.

A superset can only have more bits set, so a bit present in macrostate_signature(a) and absent from macrostate_signature(b) exhibits a state of a that is missing from b and proves a ⊄ b. The converse does not hold: states that are congruent modulo 64 share a bit, so equal signatures prove nothing. The filter therefore only ever rejects, which is what the antichain subsumption tests need to stay sound.

Nfa concatenate_eps(const Nfa &lhs, const Nfa &rhs, const Symbol &epsilon, bool use_epsilon = false, StateRenaming *lhs_state_renaming = nullptr, StateRenaming *rhs_state_renaming = nullptr)¶

Concatenate two NFAs.

Connects lhs and rhs by adding ε-transitions from each final state of lhs to each initial state of rhs. The ε is set to epsilon. If use_epsilon is false, remove_epsilon(epsilon) is run on the result, so every transition over epsilon disappears, including the operands’ own transitions labelled with that symbol. Operand transitions over any other symbol are preserved; in particular, with epsilon != EPSILON the operands’ EPSILON transitions survive, which is not the case when epsilon == EPSILON.

Parameters:

  • lhs – [in] First automaton to concatenate.

  • rhs – [in] Second automaton to concatenate.

  • epsilon – [in] Symbol used for the connecting transitions between lhs and rhs.

  • use_epsilon – [in] Whether to keep the connecting epsilon transitions in the result.

  • lhs_state_renaming – [out] Map mapping lhs states to result states.

  • rhs_state_renaming – [out] Map mapping rhs states to result states.

Returns:

Concatenated automaton.

Nfa concatenate_eps(Nfa &&lhs, const Nfa &rhs, const Symbol &epsilon, bool use_epsilon = false, StateRenaming *lhs_state_renaming = nullptr, StateRenaming *rhs_state_renaming = nullptr)¶

Concatenate two NFAs with epsilon transitions, consuming the left operand.

The left operand’s state posts are moved into the result. The right operand is copied normally. If lhs and rhs are aliased, a controlled snapshot of rhs is taken and the operation falls back to the lvalue path. lhs is left valid but empty after the operation.

Nfa concatenate_eps(Nfa &&lhs, Nfa &&rhs, const Symbol &epsilon, bool use_epsilon = false, StateRenaming *lhs_state_renaming = nullptr, StateRenaming *rhs_state_renaming = nullptr)¶

Concatenate two NFAs with epsilon transitions, consuming both operands.

The state posts of both operands are moved into the result. If lhs and rhs are aliased, a controlled snapshot of rhs is taken before lhs is consumed, so the result holds both copies. Both lhs and rhs are left valid but empty after the operation.

Nfa quotient_by_simulation(const Nfa &nfa, const Simlib::Util::BinaryRelation &sim_relation, const std::vector<size_t> &quot_proj, const BoolVector *states = nullptr, StateRenaming *state_renaming = nullptr)¶

Quotient an NFA, or a successor-closed part of it, by its forward simulation.

Each class of states equivalent under sim_relation becomes one state; its transitions are those of the class representative, without targets simulated by another target over the same symbol. With states set, only those states are kept and the representative of a class is its smallest kept state. Since forward simulation does not depend on the initial states, one relation then serves every part reachable from a single state.

Parameters:

  • nfa – [in] NFA to quotient.

  • sim_relation – [in] Forward simulation of nfa, as computed by compute_relation().

  • quot_proj – [in] Projection of each state of nfa to the smallest state of its class, as computed by get_symmetric_quotient_projection() of sim_relation.

  • states – [in] States to keep; all states if nullptr. Must be closed under successors.

  • state_renaming – [out] Map mapping the kept states to the reduced states, if not nullptr.

Returns:

The quotient of nfa restricted to states.

  • type – [in] Type of the residual construction (values: “after”, “with”).

  • direction – [in] Direction of the residual construction (values: “forward”, “backward”).

Nfa reduce_residual_with(const Nfa &nfa)¶

Reduce NFA using residual construction.

The residual construction of the residual automaton and the removal of the covering states is done during the last determinization.

Similar performance to reduce_residual_after(). The output is almost the same except the transitions: transitions may slightly differ, but the number of states is the same for both algorithm types.

Nfa reduce_residual_after(const Nfa &nfa)¶

Reduce NFA using residual construction.

The residual construction of the residual automaton and the removal of the covering states is done after the final determinization.

Similar performance to reduce_residual_with(). The output is almost the same except the transitions: transitions may slightly differ, but the number of states is the same for both algorithm types.

Nfa reduce_sat(const Nfa &nfa, const std::string &type = "nfa", const std::string &solver = "")¶

Reduce NFA to an automaton with the minimum number of states using an external SAT solver.

Experimental. A counterexample-guided search: for k = 1, 2, …, a SAT solver looks for an automaton with k states consistent with a set of sample words, the candidate is checked for equivalence with nfa, and a distinguishing word is added to the samples until the candidate is equivalent or no k-state automaton exists. The search is exponential in the worst case and is practical only for languages whose minimal automata have about ten states.

Epsilon transitions over EPSILON are removed first. The result uses the symbols and the alphabet of nfa.

Parameters:

  • nfa – [in] NFA to reduce.

  • type – [in] Kind of the resulting automaton (values: “nfa”, “dfa”):

    • ”nfa”: an NFA with the minimum number of states. It never has more states than nfa reduced by simulation.

    • ”dfa”: a deterministic (not necessarily complete) automaton with the minimum number of states.

  • solver – [in] Command running a SAT solver, as the solver’s executable followed by its arguments separated by spaces. Parts containing spaces can be enclosed in single or double quotes; the command is not interpreted by a shell otherwise. The solver is given a DIMACS CNF file as its last argument and has to print the result in the format of the SAT competitions, that is, an “s SATISFIABLE” or “s UNSATISFIABLE” line and the model on “v” lines. If empty, the value of the environment variable MATA_SAT_SOLVER is used and, if that is not set, the first of cadical, kissat, cryptominisat5 and picosat found in PATH.

Throws:

  • ExternalSolverNotFound – If no SAT solver can be found or run.

  • std::runtime_error – If the solver fails or its output cannot be understood.

Returns:

An automaton equivalent to nfa with the minimum number of states of the given type.

Nfa reduce_qbf(const Nfa &nfa, const std::string &solver = "")¶

Reduce NFA to an NFA with the minimum number of states using an external QBF solver.

Experimental. The same search as reduce_sat() with type “nfa”, but the sample words that the NFA has to reject are encoded with universally quantified runs instead of the reachable states of their prefixes.

Parameters:

  • nfa – [in] NFA to reduce.

  • solver – [in] Command running a QBF solver, given as for reduce_sat(). The solver is given a QDIMACS file as its last argument and has to print the result and the values of the outermost existential variables in the QDIMACS output format (“s cnf 1 …” or “s cnf 0 …” and “V” lines). If empty, the value of the environment variable MATA_QBF_SOLVER is used and, if that is not set, the first of depqbf and caqe found in PATH (run with --qdo, and DepQBF also with --no-dynamic-nenofex if it supports the option).

Throws:

  • ExternalSolverNotFound – If no QBF solver can be found or run.

  • std::runtime_error – If the solver fails or its output cannot be understood.

Returns:

An NFA equivalent to nfa with the minimum number of states.

Nfa construct(const mata::parser::ParsedSection &parsec, Alphabet *alphabet, NameStateMap *state_map = nullptr)¶

Loads an automaton from a single parsed section of the mata format.

Unlike the IntermediateAut overload below, this one reads parsec verbatim: Initial and Final are taken as plain lists of state names and a body line is always a source symbol target triple. State names are therefore arbitrary strings, not subject to the q/a/n naming markers or to the Boolean formulas that IntermediateAut parses; symbol names are still resolved through alphabet, which decides which of them are valid. The two overloads consequently accept different inputs and cannot be merged: routing this one through IntermediateAut would subject the state names to the naming mode of the section (with the default States marked naming rejecting every name not starting with q) and would renumber states, as the IntermediateAut path collects names from an unordered set.

Parameters:

state_map – If not nullptr, the map from state names to states, which all overloads and readers fill in the same way. The names it maps beforehand keep their states, each allocated when the input uses its name; a final formula of an IntermediateAut that is true or negates states uses every name of the map it does not negate. Every other name gets the lowest state that the automaton does not have yet and that no name of the map had beforehand, so that it never shares the state of a mapped name, used later or not at all.

Nfa create_from_regex(const std::string &regex, bool reduce = true)¶

Create NFA from regex.

The created NFA does not contain epsilons and is trimmed; with reduce, it is also reduced by simulation reduction. It uses the parser from RE2, see mata/parser/re2praser.hh for more details and options.

At https://github.com/google/re2/wiki/Syntax, you can find the syntax of regex with following further limitations: 1) The allowed characters are the first 256 characters of Unicode, i.e., Latin1 encoding (ASCII + 128 more characters). For the full Unicode, check mata/parser/re2praser.hh. 2) The created automaton represents the language of the regex and is not expected to be used in regex matching. Therefore, stuff like ^, $, , etc. are ignored in the regex. For example, the regular expressions a*b and ^a*b will both result in the same NFA accepting the language of multiple ‘a’s followed by one ‘b’. See also issue #494.

See also

mata::parser::create_nfa()

Parameters:

  • regex – regular expression

  • reduce – whether to reduce the NFA using simulation reduction; costly for large regexes

class BitvectorNfaReader
#include <builder.hh>

Reads NFAs with bitvector alphabets (@NFA-bits) over one shared set of minterms, as the general reader followed by Mintermization::mintermize() of all of them together does, but without the intermediate representations.

Transitions whose formulas are the usual Boolean combinations of symbols are read directly into BDDs. Any other @NFA-bits input goes through the general reader inside add(), so that all added automata still share one partition. The NFAs are the ones parse_from_mata() has always returned, except that the initial and the listed final states are numbered in the order of the input.

class ProcessedAntichain
#include <antichain-inclusion.hh>

The macrostates already processed for one state of the smaller automaton, bucketed by cardinality.

All entries stored here share the same state of the smaller automaton, so the dominance relation reduces to set inclusion between the macrostates of the bigger automaton. Cardinality alone then decides which entries can possibly be related to a candidate succ:

  • anti ⊆ succ requires |anti| ≤ |succ|, so the subsumption test reads nothing above |succ|;

  • succ ⊆ d requires |d| ≥ |succ|, so pruning reads nothing below |succ|;

  • at equal cardinality both reduce to equality, which is one comparison of two sorted vectors, and an entry equal to succ subsumes it, so pruning never has to consider that bucket. Inside a bucket the stored signature rejects most of the remaining pairs in O(1), before the node is read and the two sorted vectors are merged; see algorithms::macrostate_signature().

Only cardinalities that actually hold an entry get a bucket, kept in increasing order: the macrostates of one run occupy few distinct cardinalities out of the |bigger| possible ones, so indexing by cardinality would pay for (and scan) a bucket header per unused size.

Every node on the worklist is stored here as well, so marking the pruned nodes as dominated also removes them from the worklist, without scanning it.

enum class CompositionNormalization : std::uint8_t¶

How compose() normalizes its result after the construction.

Every mode keeps the relation and the level of every state; state numbering is not part of the contract, and neither is the placement of EPSILON, which are_equivalent() reads as a letter.

Values:

enumerator None¶

Return the result as constructed (trimmed when the synchronization levels are projected out). Rewrite only the states the fast composer generated itself (EPSILON padding, bridges over a replaced synchronization, and waiting states): close the whole-round EPSILON runs through generated states with exactly one incoming and one outgoing transition, outside EPSILON cycles and where the result does not grow, then merge generated states of the same level with the same outgoing transitions. Near-linear in the generated states and their transitions. The general composition generates no such states and is left as constructed.

enumerator GeneratedOnly¶
enumerator Full¶

GeneratedOnly, then the generic remove_epsilon() (with JumpMode::NoJump only, as it reads every transition as one level long), Nft::trim() and simulation-based reduce(). Far more expensive than the composition itself; only for callers who want the smallest result.

enumerator Auto¶

None: GeneratedOnly costs more in the composition than it saves in a following composition on the transducers of string constraints, whose results it shrinks by a few percent.

enumerator Trim¶

None, then trimmed, also when the synchronization levels are kept. The fast composer then builds the result forward and from the final states (by composing the reverted operands) in turns with a growing state budget and keeps whichever finishes first: on the transducers of string constraints, either direction can build tens of times more states that the trim removes than the other. Under None and Auto it builds forward only, which is cheaper when the forward direction wins, as it does on most compositions. Operands it reads through the cursors of their jump transitions are composed forward only.

Nft union_nondet(Nft &&lhs, const Nft &rhs)

Compute non-deterministic union, consuming lhs.

The left operand’s state posts are moved into the result, so no deep copy of lhs occurs. The right operand is copied normally. If lhs and rhs are aliased, a snapshot of rhs is taken before lhs is consumed, so the result holds both copies. lhs is left valid but empty after the operation.

Returns:

Non-deterministic union of lhs and rhs.

Nft union_nondet(Nft &&lhs, Nft &&rhs)

Compute non-deterministic union, consuming both operands.

Both operands’ state posts are moved into the result. If lhs and rhs are aliased, a snapshot of rhs is taken before lhs is consumed, so the result holds both copies. Both lhs and rhs are left valid but empty after the operation.

Non-deterministic union of lhs and rhs.

Nft compose(const Nft &lhs, const Nft &rhs, const utils::OrdVector<Level> &lhs_sync_levels, const utils::OrdVector<Level> &rhs_sync_levels, bool project_out_sync_levels = true, JumpMode jump_mode = JumpMode::RepeatSymbol, CompositionMode composition_mode = CompositionMode::Auto, CompositionNormalization normalization = CompositionNormalization::Auto)

Composes two NFTs.

This function computes the composition of two NFTs, lhs and rhs, by aligning their synchronization levels. Vectors of synchronization levels must be non-empty and of the same size. The levels of the resulting NFT are formed, iteratively, from the non-synchronizing levels of lhs, followed by the non-synchronizing levels of rhs, followed by the next synchronizing level (if not projected out by setting project_out_sync_levels to true). For example, given lhs with 7 levels, rhs with 8 levels, lhs_sync_levels=<0,2,5>, rhs_sync_levels=<1,4,5>, the resulting NFT levels will correspond to (assuming that we are not projecting out the synchronized levels)

  • rhs level 0

  • synchronized level from level 0 of lhs and level 1 of rhs

  • lhs level 1

  • rhs levels 2 and 3

  • synchronized level from level 2 of lhs and level 4 of rhs

  • lhs levels 3 and 4

  • synchronized level from level 5 of lhs and level 5 of rhs

  • lhs level 6

  • rhs levels 6 and 7

Parameters:

  • lhs – [in] First transducer to compose.

  • rhs – [in] Second transducer to compose.

  • lhs_sync_levels – [in] Ordered vector of synchronization levels of the lhs.

  • rhs_sync_levels – [in] Ordered vector of synchronization levels of the rhs.

  • project_out_sync_levels – [in] Whether we want to project out the synchronization levels.

  • jump_mode – [in] Specifies if the symbol on a jump transition (a transition with a length greater than 1) is interpreted as a sequence repeating the same symbol or as a single instance of the symbol followed by a sequence of DONT_CARE.

  • composition_mode – [in] Mode of composition to use. Default is Auto, which takes FastNoJump for one synchronization level per NFT when jump_mode is NoJump, or when neither NFT has a jump transition, EPSILON or DONT_CARE (the jump mode then does not matter), and General otherwise. General mode supports all NFTs, while FastNoJump mode is optimized for NFTs without jump transitions and with only one synchronization level.

  • normalization – [in] How to normalize the result after the construction; see CompositionNormalization.

Throws:

std::invalid_argument – When the request violates the precondition above, when composition_mode is FastNoJump and jump_mode is not NoJump, or when FastNoJump is asked for more than one synchronization level.

Pre:

The synchronization level vectors are non-empty, of equal size and strictly increasing, every level is below its operand’s levels.num_of_levels, and the composition leaves at least one level; otherwise std::invalid_argument naming the violated condition is thrown, in Release builds too.

Returns:

A new NFT after the composition.

std::shared_ptr<mata::AlphabetLevels> compose_alphabets(const Nft &lhs, const Nft &rhs, const utils::OrdVector<Level> &lhs_sync_levels, const utils::OrdVector<Level> &rhs_sync_levels, bool project_out_sync_levels = true)

Compose the per-level alphabets for NFTs to be composed.

Carries through the alphabet for each output level from whichever side (lhs / rhs) that level came from, in the same block order used to align levels for composition (non-synchronization levels from lhs, then from rhs, then the synchronization level itself, repeated per synchronization block, with a trailing block of remaining non-synchronization levels after the last synchronization level).

The synchronization levels of lhs and rhs must share the same alphabet instance when the synchronization levels are kept (project_out_sync_levels is false) and both alphabets are non-null.

Parameters:

  • lhs – [in] First transducer whose alphabets to compose.

  • rhs – [in] Second transducer whose alphabets to compose.

  • lhs_sync_levels – [in] Ordered vector of synchronization levels of the lhs.

  • rhs_sync_levels – [in] Ordered vector of synchronization levels of the rhs.

  • project_out_sync_levels – [in] Whether we want to project out the synchronization levels.

Throws:

std::invalid_argument – On the same invalid requests as compose(), and when the kept synchronization levels do not share an alphabet instance.

Returns:

nullptr if either lhs.alphabets or rhs.alphabets is nullptr.

Composes two NFTs with a single synchronization level.

The levels of the resulting NFT are in the following order:

General mode supports all NFTs, while FastNoJump mode is optimized for NFTs without jump transitions and with only one synchronization level.

Concatenate two NFTs, consuming the left operand.

The left operand’s state posts are moved into the result. The right operand is copied normally. If lhs and rhs are aliased, a controlled snapshot of rhs is taken before lhs is consumed. lhs is left valid but empty after the operation.

Concatenate two NFTs, consuming both operands.

The state posts of both operands are moved into the result. If lhs and rhs are aliased, a controlled snapshot of rhs is taken before lhs is consumed, so the result holds both copies. Both lhs and rhs are left valid but empty after the operation.

Perform equivalence check of two NFTs: lhs and rhs.

The current implementation of Nft does not accept input alphabet. For this reason, an alphabet has to be created from all transitions each time an operation on alphabet is called. When calling this function, the alphabet has to be computed first.

Hence, this function is less efficient than its alternative taking already defined alphabet as its parameter. That way, alphabet has to be computed only once, as opposed to the current ad-hoc construction of the alphabet. The use of the alternative with defined alphabet should be preferred.

Parameters:

  • lhs – [in] First automaton to concatenate.

  • rhs – [in] Second automaton to concatenate.

  • jump_mode – [in] Specifies if the symbol on a jump transition (a transition with a length greater than 1) is interpreted as a sequence repeating the same symbol or as a single instance of the symbol followed by a sequence of DONT_CARE symbols.

Nft invert_levels(const Nft &aut, JumpMode jump_mode = JumpMode::RepeatSymbol)

Inverts the levels of the given transducer aut.

The function inverts the levels of the transducer, i.e., the level 0 becomes the last level, level 1 becomes the second last level, and so on.

The segment between two level-zero states is read backwards, so an inner state is split by the context (state, head, tail) it is used in: one inverted state per inner state that lies on some head -> tail path. Sharing an inverted state across contexts would add tuples the original does not have (see the comment at the construction), sharing inside one context cannot. The result therefore grows with the input and the number of contexts, not with the number of paths.

Parameters:

  • aut – [in] The transducer for inverting levels. Must be layered: every transition out of a state with a nonzero level reaches a strictly higher level or level 0, and every level is below levels.num_of_levels.

  • jump_mode – [in] Specifies if the symbol on a jump transition (a transition with a length greater than 1) is interpreted as a sequence repeating the same symbol or as a single instance of the symbol followed by a sequence of DONT_CARE symbols.

Throws:

std::invalid_argument – If aut is not layered, i.e., if some segment between two level-zero states contains a cycle or a transition that does not increase the level.

Returns:

A new transducer with inverted levels.

Nft remove_epsilon(const Nft &aut, Symbol epsilon = EPSILON)

Remove simple epsilon transitions.

Simple epsilon transitions are the transitions of the form q0 -epsilon-> q1 -epsilon-> q2 -epsilon-> … -epsilon-> qn where q0 and qn are level 0 states, the states in-between are states with level 1, 2, …, num_of_levels and for each qi, for 0 < i < n, there is only 1 transition going to qi (the transition qi-1 -epsilon-> qi) and only 1 transition going from qi (the transition qi -epsilon -> qi+1). This means that if there was some state p0 going with epsilon to q1, these to epsilon transitions would not be removed.

Furthermore, this assumes that the NFT aut does not have jump transitions.

The resulting automaton has the same number of states as aut, just the transitions can change. It is recommended to run trim() after this function.

Parameters:

  • aut – NFT without jump transitions

  • epsilon – symbol representing epsilon

Returns:

NFT whose language is same as aut but does not contain simple epsilon transitions

Nft insert_levels(const Nft &nft, const BoolVector &new_levels_mask, const std::vector<std::shared_ptr<Alphabet>> &new_level_alphabets = {}, JumpMode jump_mode = JumpMode::RepeatSymbol)

Inserts new levels, as specified by the mask new_levels_mask, into the given transducer nft.

num_of_levels must be greater than 0. The vector new_levels_mask must be nonempty, its length must be greater than num_of_levels, and it must contain exactly num_of_levels occurrences of false.

Parameters:

  • nft – [in] The original transducer.

  • new_levels_mask – [in] A mask representing the old and new levels. The vector {1, 0, 1, 1, 0} indicates that one level is inserted before level 0 and two levels are inserted before level 1.

  • new_level_alphabets – [in] Alphabets to assign to the newly-inserted levels, in the order the levels appear (i.e., aligned with the true entries of new_levels_mask from left to right). Only meaningful when nft.alphabets is in AlphabetLevels::Mode::MultiLevel (ignored, and may be left empty, in Global mode, since a single shared alphabet already applies to every level). When empty (the default), the newly-inserted levels are left without an alphabet (nullptr), matching the previous behaviour.

  • jump_mode – [in] Specifies whether the symbol on a jump transition (a transition with a length greater than 1) is interpreted as a sequence repeating the same symbol or as a single instance of the symbol followed by a sequence of DONT_CARE symbols.

Throws:

std::invalid_argument – If new_level_alphabets is nonempty and its size does not match the number of newly-inserted levels (i.e., the number of true entries in new_levels_mask).

Inserts a new level new_level into the given transducer nft.

num_of_levels must be greater than 0.

If new_level is less than num_of_levels, then it is inserted before the level new_level-1. If new_level is greater than or equal to num_of_levels, then all levels from num_of_levels through new_level are appended after the last level.

When nullptr (the default), the newly-inserted level is left without an alphabet, matching the previous behaviour.
